> **What this case shows** — stand on foam and you sway more: the compliant surface degrades ankle
> proprioception, so balance leans on vision and the vestibular system, and the center of pressure travels
> farther. This case demonstrates and certifies that across a real 50-subject cohort. Per subject, COP
> path length on firm and foam ground comes from the **certified** `swayMetrics`; a newly-authored
> **`pairedTTest`** compares them, reproducing **`scipy.stats.ttest_rel`** *and* base R
> **`t.test(paired = TRUE)`** **bit-for-bit**. Foam sway is **~2.8x** firm, and foam beats firm in **all
> 50 of 50 subjects**.

::: {.callout-tip title="The recipe you'll learn"}
**Workflow** — `pairedTTest(x, y)` → the paired t-statistic, p-value and df for matched measurements.
**Way of thinking** — chain validated ops: certify the per-trial metric (`swayMetrics` vs Prieto), then
certify the group test (`pairedTTest` vs scipy/base R). The effect you report then rests on two
bit-for-bit foundations, not one.
**Ecosystem usage** — `PhysioAnalysis::pairedTTest()`, `PhysioMoCap::swayMetrics()`.
:::

## Proposition

Across 50 subjects, COP path length is greater on foam than firm ground (mean 167 vs 61 cm, ratio 2.76 of
the group means; all 50/50 subjects); the paired t-test (t = 17.3, df = 49, p ~ 1.6e-22) reproduces
`scipy.stats.ttest_rel` and base R `t.test(paired = TRUE)` bit-for-bit.

## Question & goal

**The question is a cohort effect and a chained certification: does the shipped `swayMetrics` path length
capture the foam-vs-firm sensory-reweighting effect, and does a newly-authored paired t-test reproduce
the reference?** The goal is to certify `pairedTTest`, reuse the already-certified `swayMetrics`, and
quantify the effect.

## Challenge & approach

For each subject we take the eyes-open firm and eyes-open foam quiet-standing trials, compute the COP path
length with `swayMetrics` (certified against the Prieto reference in the
[sway-posturography-bds](../sway-posturography-bds/index.qmd) case), and compare the 50 paired values with
`pairedTTest`, checking the statistic and p against `scipy.stats.ttest_rel` and base R.

```
50 subjects × {firm, foam} COP → swayMetrics path length (certified) → 50 paired values
  firm mean 61 cm   ·   foam mean 167 cm   ·   ratio 2.76 (all 50/50 foam > firm)
  pairedTTest → t = 17.3, df = 49, p ~ 1.6e-22   vs scipy.stats.ttest_rel & base R → |diff| = 0
```

## Data

**Santos & Duarte (2016) balance dataset (figshare)**: 50 subjects, one eyes-open firm and one eyes-open
foam quiet-standing trial each (60 s, force-plate COP at 100 Hz). Details in
[`artifacts/data_sources.json`](artifacts/data_sources.json).

## Results

![Left: every subject's COP path length rises from firm to foam (each faint line a subject; all 50 go up), the group mean (red) climbing 61→167 cm. Right: the distribution of per-subject foam/firm ratios — all above 1 (mean of the individual ratios ~2.9; the ratio of the group means is 2.76). The paired t-test gives t = 17.3, p ~ 1.6e-22.](artifacts/figure.png)

*How to read this:* left — the effect is not just a mean shift, it is universal: no subject sways less on
foam. Right — the ratio is centered well above 1, the size of the proprioceptive contribution.

| Quantity | Value |
|---|--:|
| mean firm / foam path length | 61 / 167 cm |
| **foam / firm ratio** (of group means) | **2.76** |
| subjects with foam > firm | **50 / 50** |
| **paired t** (df 49) | **17.3** |
| −log₁₀ p | 21.8 (p ~ 1.6e-22) |
| vs `scipy.stats.ttest_rel` / base R (\|diff\|) | **0** (bit-for-bit) |

The paired test equals both references exactly, and the effect is universal. Values trace to
[`artifacts/pairedt_summary.csv`](artifacts/pairedt_summary.csv).

## Conclusion

`pairedTTest` is certified against two references, and it rests on the already-certified `swayMetrics`.
The transferable takeaway: **balance depends on proprioception — remove reliable foot-surface cues (stand
on foam) and sway roughly triples, in every subject. This is why foam-surface posturography is a standard
probe of the somatosensory contribution to standing, and why the firm-vs-foam contrast is a workhorse of
fall-risk assessment.**

## Open questions

- This uses one eyes-open trial per surface and the path-length metric; the BDS also has eyes-closed
  trials, three trials per condition, and the full Prieto metric set, supporting a two-way (vision ×
  surface) repeated-measures analysis. The paired foam-vs-firm contrast shown here is the largest, most
  reliable single effect. *Documented, not escalated.*

## Using this in your own analysis

| Step | Function | Package |
|---|---|---|
| Paired-samples t-test | `pairedTTest()` | PhysioAnalysis |
| Posturography sway metrics | `swayMetrics()` | PhysioMoCap |

**Reading the result.**

- **t / p** — the paired t tests whether the within-subject difference is systematically non-zero; here it
  is, overwhelmingly.
- **ratio and n foam>firm** — report the effect size (foam/firm) and its universality alongside the
  p-value; a significant p with a small or inconsistent effect would be far weaker evidence.

**The recipe, copy-runnable:**

```r
library(PhysioAnalysis); library(PhysioMoCap)

firm <- swayMetrics(cop_firm, 100)$path_length   # per subject, per surface
foam <- swayMetrics(cop_foam, 100)$path_length
pairedTTest(foam, firm)                          # t, p, df -- reproduces scipy/base R bit-for-bit
```

**Auditing the numbers.** Every value on this page traces to
[`artifacts/pairedt_summary.csv`](artifacts/pairedt_summary.csv), and [`audit.py`](audit.py) re-checks the
paired t and p, the bit-exact match against scipy and base R, `df = n − 1`, the universal foam > firm
direction, the effect size, and the honestly noted scope (new paired-test op; the input path lengths come
from the certified swayMetrics; the sensory-reweighting interpretation).
